items.note: Ganguly: the list of poets Merutunga gives as Bhoja's contemporaries is incredible chronologically; many flourished long before Bhoja
Ganguly finds the Bhojacharita list of Bhoja's contemporary poets erroneous but holds that many poets flourished under his patronage; H.C. Ray agrees that numerous scholars worked under Bhoja
Dhanapala is the earliest known literary man attached to Bhoja's court, flourishing at the end of the 10th and beginning of the 11th century
Bhoja impressed by Dhanapala's brilliance and made him patron poet; Ain-i-Akbari ranks him next after Vararuchi among the 500 poets of Bhoja's court
Dhanapala's first work was composed in Sam 1029 (A.D. 972) while he resided at Dhara
Dhanika, settled in Malwa before Sam 1031 (974 A.D.), was connected with the administrative department of the Paramara Utpalaraja
Padmagupta, court poet of Sindhuraja, refers to the poetess Sita in the context of king Upendra (Krsnaraja, the first king) of the Paramara dynasty
Poetess Sita placed in the context of king Upendra (Krsnaraja the first king) of the Paramara dynasty; Ganguly thinks the two Sitas identical
Sita wrote a prasasti on Upendra's exploits; the Jain author mistakenly places her in Bhoja's reign, so her presence at Bhoja's court is called imaginary
First two acts of Madana's drama Parijatamanjari are inscribed in the Bhojasala at Dhara, later converted by Muslims into the Kamal mosque; first played at Dhara
Parijatamanjari praises the Paramara king Arjunavarma in his war with Jayasimha of Gujarat; Arjunavarma alive V.S. 1267 (A.D. 1210), so Madana is much later than Bhoja
Grammatical rules engraved by Bhoja on the walls of the university at Dhara were popular from Kashmir to Maharashtra
Assessments of Bhoja: Col. James on his name enduring while Hindu literature survives; Josyer calls him an erudite and enlightened sovereign of Malwa with almost mythical fame as a patron
Chief architectural characteristics of the period: emphasised treatment of wall surfaces and sculpture covering the whole exterior with decorative richness
Parts of each medieval temple: vimana, sikhara, garbhagriha (womb house), mandapa as pillared assembly hall
Antarala as vestibule uniting sanctuary and hall; ardhamandapa porch; mahamandapa as central hall
Nagara temple with sikhara; the northern sikhara said to develop from the Buddhist stupa, via chaitya, to the tower
Trident on the finial marks a Siva temple, with a linga in the cella and Nandi bull outside in front of the entrance
Temple edifice normally faces east so morning sun penetrates the sanctum
Temple architecture guided by fundamental principles and technical codes, coordinated by sreni guilds and silpa canons
Samarangana Sutradhara is a great contemporary silpa-sastra work in two volumes dealing with sculpture, painting and architecture
The vastu-sastra portion contains detailed directions for constructing every kind of religious and secular building, with rules of proportion and astronomical calculations
Early sources classify sanctuaries as Nagara (Himalayas to Vindhyas), Dravida and Besara (Vindhyas to Krishna, central India)
Northern Nagara temples have a lofty ribbed curvilinear spire surmounted by amalaka and kalasa
Nagara plan is square with graduated projections giving a cruciform shape; the tower inclines in a convex curve with the projections carried upward
According to the unpublished Aparajita-priccha the Nagara type is native of Madhyadesa, though few northern examples survive except Khajuraho
Paramaras of Malwa were great builders of Siva temples; Bhoja built temples dedicated to Kedaresvara, Ramesvara, Somanatha, Sundira(?) and Kalanala Rudra
Footnote cites the Udaipur Prasasti (E.I. I, p. 238, v. 20) for Bhoja's temples; Upadhye and Jain read Kala-Anala-Rudra as Kalagni-Rudra, a terrible form of Siva
refs: Udaipur Prasasti, E.I. I p. 238 v. 20
Upadhye and Jain, Yasastilaka and Indian Culture p. 471

items.note: Bhojesvara Siva temple at Bhojpur, 20 miles south of Bhopal, a significant Paramara temple of Malwa, presumed late 11th or 12th century
The Udayesvara or Nilakanthesvara temple was built by the Paramara king Udayaditya at Udayapur in the old Gwalior state
Sanctum and mandapa rise on a high adhisthana; sanctum has a sikhara, mandapa a pyramidal roof; exterior of sanctum in foliated star-shaped plan from rotating squares

claim.value: described as 'Nagara' temple style of Dekkan

items.note: Plinth mouldings have a general likeness to Khajuraho temples, but the design on the whole follows the typical Dakhanese version

claim.value: mouldings like Khajuraho but overall design typically Dakhanese

items.note: Chases in the jangha are faceted pilasters, angular because of the star-shaped plan, each with sculpture on both sides, ending in capital mouldings and a cornice as transition to the sikhara
Sikhara rises with slight curvature above unbroken vertical spines, repeating the vertical and horizontal themes of the cube below
Percy Brown sees an affinity of the Udayapura temple to the Chandella group at Khajuraho; S.K. Sarasvati disagrees, arguing the design is pre-eminently Dakhanese

claim.value: Brown: affinity to Chandella (Khajuraho) group; Sarasvati: pre-eminently Dakhanese

refs: S.K. Sarasvati, Struggle for Empire p. 697 fn

items.note: Stella Kramrisch: great correspondence of structure and superstructure, the bisama repeating the five-pointed star and the amalaka-sila responding to the star-shaped temple
refs: Stella Kramrisch, Hindu Temples II p. 391

items.note: Mandapa roof pyramidal in tiers; mighty gable over the antarala links the two divergent superstructures; entire monument a unified design
Temples at Arang, Rahilya and Savari-Narayana near Kharod show Dakhanese features but not as completely as the Nilakanthesvara at Udayapura

claim.value: Dakhanese features, most complete at Nilakanthesvara, Udayapura

items.note: Samarangana-Sutradhara defines a capital and prescribes town fortification of five parts: moats and ramparts, parapets, towers and turrets, gateways, and highways
An ideal town to have 3 or 4 principal roads each way; two king's highways crossing at the centre, 36 feet wide in a first-grade town
Samarangana-Sutradhara fixes residence by profession and caste (jativarnadhivasa); four castes dwell in different quarters; the central part of the capital is the palace area
Samarangana-Sutradhara refers to small, middle and big palaces for gods, king and Brahmana, in three kinds: Ruchaka, Dravida and Meru
Samarangana-Sutradhara gives the Meru palace as Prasadaraja (king of palaces) with area of 33 to 50 hands and sikhara one-tenth of the whole
Samarangana-Sutradhara deals in detail with construction of ordinary houses, generally well-roofed

Dwelling house generally faced east, with compound wall, courtyard, staircase, two storeys and terrace; water fetched from a common well probably dug by the king or a rich person, plus a rain-water reservoir
